newsitem.title: UK: Client screening a must for financiers warns SFA.
newsitem.headline: Client screening a must for financiers warns SFA.

text.p: Taking on the wrong clients is a danger facing many corporate finance players, the head of British financial watchdog the Securities and Futures Authority said on Tuesday.
Richard Farrant, SFA chief executive, told a conference on regulating corporate finance that the "reputational risk of acting for sharp clients" was particularly acute for smaller firms.
These were more desperate to gain new business and might therefore be less diligent in screening potential new clients before working for them.

But Farrant also highlighted the dangers faced by larger corporate finance houses when he referred to British merchant bank Hambros and its recent role in advising on the failed bid for Britain's Co-operative Wholesale Society (CWS).
"I wouldn't be surprised now if Hambros didn't slightly regret not screening clients and their sources of information more closely," Farrant said.
Last month Hambros made an unreserved apology to the CWS for its conduct in advising entrepreneur Andrew Regan in his audacious but now discredited 1.2 billion pound ($1.9 billion) takeover plan.

CWS dropped legal action against Hambros after the apology and a substantial financial settlement. Hambros has severed its links with Regan, his Guernsey-based investment trust Lanica and the Galileo special bidding vehicle.

Hambros has appointed City law firm Norton Rose to undertake an inquiry into the affair and Peter Large, the senior corporate financier responsible for the bid, has requested "to be relieved of his executive responsibilities for the time being" to enable him to concentrate on the probe.
SFA is monitoring the inquiry but no regulatory moves will begin before this has been completed.

Corporate finance was generally not a major worry of SFA-regulated firms, Farrant said. Of 289 firms involved in such business, less than 20 were causing significant worries in an assessment of their individual risk.
SFA has recently adopted a risk-exposure rating system for the more than 1,300 firms it regulates. Known as FIBSPAM, it has five criteria by which each firm is rated on a score of one to five.
These criteria span financial integrity, internal controls, quality of business, supervisory complexity and quality of personnel and management..

If a firm is seen as high risk, it will get frequent visits from SFA, a medium risk firm will get fewer visits while a low risk firm will get infrequent visits, possibly as rarely as every two or three years, Farrant said.
But although there were no plans to make the scores public, SFA was very strongly tempted towards informing firms of their scores on the condition that they did not publicise them.
This would enable a dialogue with the companies, which Farrant said was an important factor in regulating them effectively.
"I would want to be sure of knowing what the potential benefits or downside were before we even considered it," he said.

Apart from screening clients, potential problem areas for firms active in corporate finance work -- corporate advisory, mergers and acquisitions and arranging and advising on takeovers, bids, new issues, placing, underwriting and research -- were financial, commercial and regulatory, Farrant said.
Underwriting and sub-underwriting had both caused problems, as had accounting for fees which had not yet been received and the taking of principal positions and cash flow.

Smaller firms in particular could become over-dependent on single transactions or income sources and performance fees as well as stretching beyond their own capabilities and risking reputations by acting for unscreened clients.

At a regulatory level, Farrant highlighted Chinese walls -- which are internal barriers in companies designed to avoid conflicts of interest -- inadequate due diligence, inadequate advice and disclosure and improper marketing as other possible problem areas.
